items.t: Moderate to severe hypertension.

src.q: Treatment of moderate to severe hypertension.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK SmPC.

items.t: 250 mg two or three times daily for 2 days, then adjust every 2 days to response. Usual 500 mg-2 g daily; maximum 3 g daily. Increase the evening dose first (sedation).

src.q: 250mg 2-3 times daily for 2 days, adjusted at intervals of 2 days until adequate response is obtained. Maximum dose 3g daily (increase evening dose first). Usual effective dose 500mg to 2g daily.

items.t: Switching from other antihypertensives: withdraw those gradually; start methyldopa at no more than 500 mg daily, increasing at intervals of at least 2 days.

src.q: methyldopa should be limited to an initial dose of not more than 500 mg daily and increased as required at intervals of not less than two days.

items.t: Elderly: start no higher than 250 mg daily (e.g. 125 mg twice daily); increase slowly; maximum 2 g daily.

src.q: Initial dose should be kept as low as possible not exceeding 250mg daily. An appropriate starting dose would be 125mg twice daily, increased slowly as required but not exceeding a maximum daily dosage of 2g.

items.t: Stopping: hypertension usually returns within 48 hours (usually without overshoot).

src.q: Withdrawal of methyldopa is followed by return of hypertension, usually within 48 hours.

items.t: Children: 10 mg/kg daily in 2-4 divided doses, adjusted to response; maximum 65 mg/kg daily or 3 g daily, whichever is less.

src.q: 10mg/kg bodyweight daily in 2-4 divided doses. The dosage is increased or decreased until adequate response is achieved. Maximum recommended daily dose is 65mg/kg bodyweight or 3g whichever is less.

items.t: Hypersensitivity (including liver disorders with previous methyldopa); history of depression; active hepatic disease (e.g. acute hepatitis, active cirrhosis); MAOI therapy; porphyria. Not recommended for (and in 4.4 contraindicated in) catecholamine-secreting tumours such as phaeochromocytoma.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to methyldopa or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1 (including hepatic disorders associated with previous methyldopa therapy)
A history of depression Active hepatic disease such as acute hepatitis and active cirrhosis On therapy with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) Porphyria
Methyldopa is contraindicated for the treatment of patients with a catecholamine-secreting tumour such as phaeochromocytoma or paraganglioma.

items.t: Haemolytic anaemia (rare, deaths reported): check haemoglobin/haematocrit if anaemia is suspected and test for haemolysis; stop if haemolytic anaemia. Positive Coombs test in 10-20% (matters for blood cross-matching).

src.q: If haemolytic anaemia is present, Methyldopa tablets should be discontinued.
From the reports of different investigators, the incidence averages between 10% and 20%.

items.t: Liver: fever, abnormal liver tests or jaundice (usually in the first 2-3 months; rare fatal hepatic necrosis) - withdraw and do not use again. Use with caution if there is a history of liver disease.

src.q: Should fever, abnormality in liver function, or jaundice occur, therapy should be withdrawn.
Methyldopa should not be used again in these patients.
Methyldopa should be used with caution in patients with a history of previous liver disease or dysfunction.

items.t: Severe bilateral cerebrovascular disease: involuntary choreoathetotic movements - stop if they occur. Hepatic porphyria in the patient or near relatives: extreme caution.

src.q: Should these movements occur, therapy should be discontinued.
Methyldopa Tablets should be used with extreme caution in patients, or in near relatives of patients, with hepatic porphyria.

items.t: Anaesthesia: reduced anaesthetic doses may be needed. Dialysis removes methyldopa (hypertension may recur).

src.q: Patients may require reduced doses of anaesthetics when on methyldopa.
Dialysis removes methyldopa; therefore, hypertension may recur after this procedure.

items.t: Lab interference: urinary uric acid, serum creatinine (alkaline picrate) and AST (colorimetric); false-high urinary catecholamines. Urine may darken on standing.

src.q: Methyldopa may interfere with the measurement of urinary uric acid by the phosphotungstate method, serum creatinine by the alkaline picrate method, and AST (SGOT) by colorimetric method.

items.t: Lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: MAOIs: contraindicated; stop MAOIs before starting methyldopa.

src.q: On therapy with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors should be discontinued before treatment with methyldopa.

items.t: Other antihypertensives (and thiazide diuretics, general anaesthetics, levodopa): enhanced effect - follow progress carefully. Verapamil: may intensify sinus bradycardia.

src.q: When methyldopa is used with other antihypertensive drugs, potentiation of antihypertensive action may occur. The progress of patients should be carefully followed
Concurrent use of verapamil and methyldopa can intensify sinus bradycardia.

items.t: Iron (ferrous sulphate or gluconate): reduced methyldopa bioavailability; may worsen blood pressure control.

src.q: Several studies demonstrate a decrease in the bioavailability of methyldopa when it is ingested with ferrous sulphate or ferrous gluconate.

items.t: Sympathomimetics, tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines and MAOIs may reduce the antihypertensive effect. Lithium: monitor for lithium toxicity. Haloperidol toxicity may increase.

src.q: The antihypertensive effect of methyldopa may be diminished by sympathomimetics, tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazine derivatives and monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
When methyldopa and lithium are given concomitantly the patient should be monitored carefully for symptoms of lithium toxicity.

items.t: Largely excreted by the kidney; patients with impaired renal function may respond to smaller doses (no threshold given). Removed by dialysis.

src.q: Methyldopa is largely excreted by the kidney, and patients with impaired renal function may respond to smaller doses.

items.t: Contraindicated in active hepatic disease (acute hepatitis, active cirrhosis). Caution with a history of liver disease or dysfunction. Check liver function before and during the first 6-12 weeks.

src.q: Active hepatic disease such as acute hepatitis and active cirrhosis
Methyldopa should be used with caution in patients with a history of previous liver disease or dysfunction.

items.t: SmPC: used under close supervision for hypertension in pregnancy; no evidence of fetal abnormalities or neonatal effects, fetal harm appears remote, but cannot be excluded - weigh benefits against risks.

src.q: Methyldopa has been used under close medical supervision for the treatment of hypertension during pregnancy.
the use of the drug in women who are, or may become pregnant requires that anticipated benefits be weighed against possible risks.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concern that it harms the baby. Switch to a different medicine within a few days of delivery (risk of low mood/depression after birth).

src.q: Methyldopa can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
If you take methyldopa at the end of pregnancy, your doctor will advise that you switch to a different medicine within a few days of delivery.

items.t: Appears in breast milk; weigh anticipated benefits against possible risks.

src.q: Methyldopa appears in breast milk. The use of the drug in breast-feeding mothers requires that anticipated benefits be weighed against possible risks.

items.t: BUMPS: after birth methyldopa can increase the chance of low mood and depression; a switch is usually advised within a few days of delivery.

src.q: This is because taking methyldopa after the baby's birth can increase your chance of low mood and depression.

items.t: BUMPS: no increased risk to the baby is expected if the father takes methyldopa. The SmPC gives no fertility or contraception information.

src.q: We do not expect any increased risk to your baby if the father takes methyldopa.

items.t: Frequencies not known. Sedation (usually transient, at start or after dose increases), headache, weakness, dizziness, light-headedness, dry mouth, nasal congestion, orthostatic hypotension (reduce dose), oedema/weight gain.

src.q: Many patients experience sedation for two or three days when therapy with methyldopa is started or when the dose is increased.
Orthostatic hypotension (decrease daily dosage)

items.t: Haemolytic anaemia, bone-marrow failure, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; hepatitis/jaundice (stop; do not re-use); myocarditis, pericarditis, AV block, bradycardia; depression, psychosis; toxic epidermal necrolysis, angioedema; pancreatitis; lupus-like syndrome.

src.q: Haemolytic anaemia, bone-marrow failure, leucopenia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, eosinophilia
Rare cases of fatal hepatic necrosis have been reported.

items.t: Stop if oedema progresses or signs of heart failure appear.

src.q: (Discontinue methyldopa if oedema progresses or signs of heart failure appear.)

items.t: Liver function tests and total and differential white cell count before therapy.

src.q: Liver-function tests and a total and differential white bloodcell count are advisable before therapy and at intervals during the first six weeks to twelve weeks of therapy, or whenever an unexplained fever occurs.

items.t: Repeat liver tests and white cell count at intervals in the first 6-12 weeks and whenever unexplained fever occurs; haemoglobin/haematocrit if anaemia is suspected.

src.q: at intervals during the first six weeks to twelve weeks of therapy, or whenever an unexplained fever occurs.
should symptoms suggest anaemia, haemoglobin and/or haematocrit determinations should be made.

items.t: Stop if haemolytic anaemia, fever, abnormal liver function, jaundice or choreoathetotic movements occur.

src.q: Should fever, abnormality in liver function, or jaundice occur, therapy should be withdrawn.
If haemolytic anaemia is present, Methyldopa tablets should be discontinued.

items.t: Oral. When increasing the dose, increase the evening dose first to limit daytime sedation.

src.q: When increasing the dosage, therefore, it may be desirable to increase the evening dose first.

items.t: Drowsiness, dizziness and light-headedness can occur, especially at the start or after a dose increase; do not drive or operate machinery if affected.

src.q: If affected, patients should not attempt to drive, or operate machinery.

items.t: Report unexplained fever, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms of anaemia promptly. Urine may darken on standing (harmless).

src.q: Rarely, when urine is exposed to air after voiding, it may darken because of breakdown of methyldopa or its metabolites.
